item.itunes:author: 3C 達人廖阿輝
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CU6FI26I3zo

值得閱讀的理由

  • 快速掌握 AUKEY 三款磁吸充電新品的規格、特色與適用情境。
  • 比較 5000mAh 與 10000mAh 行動電源的攜帶性和續航取捨，協助挑選適合自己的款式。
  • 了解三合一充電器的充電能力、相容性與旅行收納設計，以及它和行動電源的差異。
  • 認識 Qi2 認證、安全防護與搭機攜帶等實用資訊。

摘要

三款新品各有定位

作者介紹 AUKEY 三款磁吸充電新品：輕薄的 MS15、大容量的 MS16，以及可同時為多種裝置充電的 MC319B。前兩款是磁吸行動電源，MC319B 則是需要外接電源的折疊式充電器。

MS15 配備5000mAh 電量，厚度約 0.9 公分、重量約 109 克，主打輕巧好攜帶。它支援最高 15W 的 Qi2 磁吸無線充電與最高 20W 有線輸出，適合日常通勤或臨時補電。

MS15 內建可調角度支架，可直立或橫放手機；機身也有數位電量顯示，並提供低電流模式，方便為低功耗裝置充電。

大容量行動電源與安全資訊

MS16 將容量提升至10000mAh，重量約 191 克，同樣支援 Qi2 15W 無線充電、20W 有線輸出，並配有折疊支架和電量顯示。作者指出，MS15 較輕薄，MS16 則適合長時間外出或用電需求較高的人。

兩款行動電源皆具備過充、過放及短路等安全防護，並通過相關認證。作者也提醒，產品規格符合隨身登機標準，但應放在隨身行李中，避免托運；實際攜帶仍可留意航空公司規定。

選購時，重視輕便與較薄手感可考慮 MS15；需要更多備用電量、能接受較高重量，則可選 MS16。

MC319B 三合一充電器

MC319B 可同時為手機、手錶與耳機充電，手機支援最高 25W Qi2 無線充電，手錶與耳機也各有專用充電位置。它不是行動電源，使用時必須連接 USB-C 電源。

作者說明，MC319B 的磁吸設計適用於 iPhone，以及具備磁吸功能或搭配磁吸配件的 Android 手機。折疊後方便收納，盒裝另附收納盒與充電線，適合整理桌面或出差旅行使用。

總結與認證查詢

作者總結，MS15 適合日常輕巧補電，MS16 適合長時間外出或重度使用者，MC319B 則適合想用單一裝置替手機、手錶和耳機充電的人。三款產品的選擇，取決於使用者更看重便攜性、電量，還是多裝置整合。

作者補充，消費者可至 WPC（無線充電聯盟）的產品資料庫查詢 Qi2 認證紀錄。認證有助確認產品符合相關充電、安全與相容性規範。

item.itunes:title: 多花近 2 萬，只為少帶一台？iPhone Duo 值不值得買
item.itunes:author: 3C 達人廖阿輝
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QL19oC8Kw3s

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析摺疊款 iPhone是否真能取代「iPhone 搭配 iPad」的雙機配置，協助消費者評估高額花費的實用價值。
  • 全面對比各種硬體組合（涵蓋 iPad mini 8 與 iPad Air）在購買預算與攜帶重量上的具體差距。
  • 詳細解析摺疊螢幕與獨立平板在多工軟體生態（iPadOS 與 iOS）及日常生活便利性上的本質不同。

摘要

雙機組合與摺疊機的價格定位對比

Reading mode is the same; you can just zoom in, and there's enough space on the sides so that you aren't left with just a small snippet after zooming. When you're watching videos, although there might be some black bars due to different aspect. ratios, the overall picture feels quite immersive. Moreover, compared to the more square-like aspect ratio of past foldables, this one feels more like a small tablet, which is much smoother to use. So, whether you're sitting in a cafe, on a commute, or lying in bed at night, once you open your iPhone foldable, it gives you that small tablet feel, making it super comfortable to use . Alright, next is gaming. Playing games on the unfolded iPhone is really satisfying. Once the screen gets bigger , the control areas don't all get crammed together, and when it's closed, the outer screen is actually already quite easy to use. Once opened, it feels like a small tablet; whether it's the. map, character skill buttons, or information panels, everything can be displayed on a larger, more comfortable screen. When playing landscape games, the wider field of view is very noticeable. In portrait games, the inner screen can also enlarge the content, making it more comfortable than a regular phone to check maps, view character info, or look at event pages. Not to mention, because of its split-screen capability, you can run Pokémon and Pikmin at the same time; this experience is truly super comfortable and satisfying. Or, you can play a game while looking at a walkthrough—this is the advantage and the extra benefit that the new aspect ratio and large screen bring. It doesn't.

just cram a phone into tablet mode; rather, it switches from a closed phone into a new space and a new way of using it that's truly suited for content and gaming, which is something a bit more special. I think saying this might be controversial and people might have issues with it, because everyone says that app support for foldables isn't great, but I want to ask in return: is this kind of resource and approach really that bad? I actually feel that if you’ve used a foldable compared to other Android devices, the effect is the best when a mobile app already supports the iPhone foldable. Let's compare them. point by point. My view is that the best support comes from apps already optimized for the iPhone Duo, followed by the current level of support found on Android devices. Of course, the worst experience is with apps that don't support the iPhone Duo; they might have black bars on the edges or lack support for full-screen orientation. But if an app is truly optimized for the iPhone Duo's specifications and guidelines regarding its inner and outer screens, it won't just scale up the interface; it will rearrange its buttons, content, and. multitasking layout. App support will take some time, as this is Apple's first foldable, but this isn't necessarily a permanent problem. Now that Apple has officially entered the foldable market, as the number of users grows, developers will naturally have the incentive to improve their apps. Many apps already provide support right from the start, such as Facebook and Netflix; these are already good to go. And this doesn't just benefit Apple. I have to say, as an Android user myself, when more developers start taking foldable screens seriously, the app ecosystem for Android. foldables will also benefit and improve . So, when I look at app support, I don't just look at which apps haven't been updated yet, because it's unreasonable to expect 100%support from the moment a new device launches. Instead, I see that once Apple expands the market, the entire foldable ecosystem will progress together, which is what I find most worth looking forward to. Alright, let's move on to the downsides. After using it, what are the things I really find hard to accept ? The first, of course, is that it really isn't light. It is genuinely heavy; there's no way around it this. time. The body alone weighs 254 grams, which is noticeably heavy right out of the box. Add to that a screen protector , a protective case, and some other accessories, and you’ll definitely feel the weight when carrying it every day. When you first get it, you might feel the build quality is great and the structure is solid—that's true—but after a week of use, the weight is something you will definitely have to consider. You'll feel it when you put it in your pocket, when you hold it to watch videos , and even after typing with one hand for a while. Especially if you were.

using a thinner, lighter slab phone before, switching to this iPhone means it won't be an easy phone to handle. I honestly understand why it has weight— it’s due to the dual-screen, battery structure, and full features. It’s actually still lighter and more compact than tablets of this size, and much lighter than them, too. But understanding that doesn't mean it isn't heavy. If you really prioritize thinness and lightness, you must check it out, feel it, and try the actual device in person before buying. For a more practical comparison, the 254-gram. weight is actually a bit heavier than the 249-gram iPhone 16 Pro Max. This leads to another issue, which is the one-handed usability caused by the folding phone's external screen. Although I love this folding point and its display effect is great, its outer screen isn't the traditional narrow, elongated type; it’s relatively wide when closed, which makes browsing, viewing photos, and typing more comfortable, especially typing. Typing is actually very comfortable compared to previous folding phones, but the range. your thumb can reach for one-handed use is reduced. My hands are quite large, and I still can't reach the far side completely, especially the buttons on the top left or right sides of the screen, or the keys furthest away on the keyboard; I can't always hit them while holding it one-handed. So, the most suitable way to use it—for a right-handed person, for example—is holding it with your left hand for most operations, and using your other hand when you need to reply to messages. It’s not like a traditional flat smartphone or a narrow-screen folding phone that's. easy to control with one hand; you still have to adjust your grip for some operations. You might need to slide your palm down or just use both hands, really . This isn't really an issue with Apple's design, but rather an inherent limitation of the wide-screen folding phone’s aspect ratio. Of course, Apple knows this, so they have actually included some additional, different options. For example, when opened, the UI—the new UI settings interface—moves the dock or the bottom UI design to the right side of the screen, which requires apps to be optimized and supported. The. benefit of this is that the top and bottom display areas can be utilized more fully, allowing content to extend vertically without too much space being taken up by the bottom controls. But one issue is that, for right-handed users, the control area on the right is usually closer to the thumb, making one-handed use smoother. However, this design— including the power button and the UI layout—is not friendly to left-handed users. If you hold the phone in your left hand, the UI on the right becomes harder to reach, and if you hold it in your right hand, there are still some control issues. So, relatively speaking.

, I feel that while previous designs— with controls in the center or bottom— were suitable for both hands, now there are more issues regarding left-handed versus right-handed habits. You could say this is an extended problem arising from Apple focusing operations on the right side to maximize the display area at the top and bottom, which makes the difference between the left and right hands much more obvious. I think, relatively speaking, this is a significant gripe I have. Apple has long provided a lot of assistance for people with disabilities and is one of the companies that values accessibility the. most—perhaps even the best, bar none. I often give the example that they have optimized features for phones and watches for users who have no hands or only one hand. Yet, for this iPhone interface, they didn't provide a more complete solution for left and right-handed users. I feel it's a bit strange that they've done so much to optimize for users with severe disabilities, but didn't think to provide more options for left-handed people. Perhaps in a future software update, they could provide options to. align things to the left or right, or simply add a "left-handed mode," or even —and this might be a simple or silly idea—allow users to flip the phone upside down to switch the orientation? Instead of forcing left-handed users to adapt to this new UI. So, I would say the iPhone's outer screen is indeed comfortable for viewing content; the aspect ratio is better for multimedia. However, one-handed operation is more difficult, which is a major trade-off between wide foldables and traditional, narrower, taller foldables. If you. mainly use your phone with two hands, or if you usually open the device to use the inner screen, this won't bother you much. But if you value one-handed messaging and are a small-phone user, I strongly recommend you go to a store or an Apple Store to try it out in person. Alright, the second drawback that I personally felt while using it is that it uses TouchID, but it doesn't offer a face unlock feature. TouchID itself isn't bad; it's placed on the side button, so whether your phone is on the. desk, in your hand, or in either hand, unlocking is actually quite okay and very convenient. However, after using it for a week, I still miss FaceID, because we are used to many operations where we just pick up the phone, take a glance, and it's unlocked. For Apple users, the iPhone now requires you to put your finger on the side button, and since you don't always pick up a foldable phone in the same orientation, sometimes you just want to quickly check a notification but have to adjust your grip or press it again to successfully unlock it. I actually feel that TouchID and FaceID could coexist; they don't conflict. Even.

if you just provided a simpler, non-payment-grade face unlock—like the common fingerprint plus face unlock combo seen on Android phones—this face unlock doesn't need to support high-security payment levels. Letting users choose based on the situation would, I think, make the overall experience much more complete. So, while the security is not an issue, the usage habits do require some readjustment. The third drawback, or rather a limitation, isn't about general app compatibility, but the issue of "dual opening" that. people often confuse and conflate. To be clear, as I mentioned before, foldable phones are great for opening two different apps side-by-side, split-screen multitasking, like Excel and email, or Safari with two windows open at once; this is system-level multitasking. But if you want to open two instances of the same app—for example, the most common example we see is wanting to log into two LINE accounts —that is a completely different thing. The main point is that Apple won't do what is common in the Android camp,. where you can install a third-party app or use a built-in system feature to allow apps that don't support dual instances to replicate themselves, usually called "app cloning" or "dual apps." Apple won't allow it; at least for now, it won't let third-party apps force another app to create a clone. In other words, just because one app wants to help you clone another, the system won't just allow it. Even if the system has split-screen now, app developers usually don't allow multiple accounts to be logged in on the same device, mainly. due to security considerations and concerns. For example, the feature everyone wants and I talk about most often is running two LINE accounts or dual SIMs simultaneously. I think this is a perfect example of something that’s hopeless and won't be provided. Anyway, those are the three most notable pros and cons after using the iPhone fold for a week. The pros are a complete feature set, the UDC matte inner screen, and both inner and outer screens supporting Pencil and MagSafe. Other phones really need to take note. Second, the aspect ratio is genuinely useful; it’s like a. foldable iPad mini. Reading manga, watching videos, and gaming are great experiences. Holding it really feels like using a 7 or 8-inch e-reader. Third , software support is worth looking forward to, especially with the Apple ecosystem, which might push apps to be even better. The app experience on the iPhone fold is undeniably the best, and this could also help drive the ecosystem for Android foldables, which is quite important. The cons are also obvious: it’s really heavy, the fingerprint scanner is decent but lacks face unlock.

, and not all apps can be opened in dual mode due to system limitations. Don't expect LINE dual-account support anytime soon; be prepared for that. If you are already an iPhone user and you have always wanted a larger screen, then the iPhone fold is something you absolutely must experience. If what you care about is being lightweight, or if you must have dual-account support for certain apps, you need to first confirm if you can accept these limitations. As for me, I will keep using it after this week because the satisfaction of reading manga and playing games on the unfolded screen is something a regular iPhone just can't replace. That wraps up my thoughts after one week of using the. iPhone fold. If you enjoyed this video, please like, subscribe, and hit the notification bell. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解如何透過夾式配件與轉接環，實現跨品牌將 vivo 增距鏡安裝至 OPPO 旗艦手機上使用。
  • 評估跨廠牌外接增距鏡在對焦速度、畫面穩定度及錄影表現上的實際可用性與限制。
  • 對比原廠 3.28 倍與 vivo 2.35 倍增距鏡的倍率差異與焦段效果，提供具性價比的鏡頭搭配參考。

摘要

跨品牌增距鏡搭配的安裝方案

作者本次進行了一場跨廠牌實測，嘗試將 vivo 2.35 倍增距鏡安裝至 OPPO Find 系列旗艦手機上。安裝方式並非硬套，而是使用橫拉式夾式配件搭配 16mm 螺紋金屬轉接環，轉接成 vivo 專用的三爪接環設計。調整好鏡頭圈位置扣上後，手機便能順利進入增距鏡模式正常運作。

實際拍攝與對焦穩定度實測

作者展示了實測照片與影片，指出實際效果出乎意料地理想。雖然在安裝便利性上略遜於原廠專用鏡頭保護殼，但由於兩者鏡頭焦段相近，無論是拍照還是錄影，其對焦速度與防手震穩定性幾乎與原廠鏡頭無異。作者特別提醒，較建議搭配一代或二代的 2.35 倍鏡頭，若使用焦段過長的版本則穩定度較難掌握。

倍率差異分析與實測總結

相較於 OPPO 原廠哈蘇增距鏡的 3.28 倍，vivo 增距鏡為 2.35 倍，在遠方主體的拉近程度上略遜一籌，但依然能顯著往前推進長焦距離。整體而言，這組跨平台的搭配在對焦、錄影及畫質穩定度上皆具備極高的可用性，對於手邊已有 vivo 增距鏡的使用者來說，是個實用且可行的外接鏡頭方案。
